title: Parental awareness, trust, and willingness to accept RSV immunization: A mixed-methods study in Chile
content:
by Alexis V. Cruz, Emilie Karafillakis, Greet Hendrickx, Alexandre De Figueiredo, Rachel Eagan, Angello Retamal, Margarita K. Lay, Mario Calvo, Claudia A. Montero-Liberona, Alexis M. Kalergis

This study examines parental awareness of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and the determinants of trust in—and willingness to accept—RSV immunization in Chile using a sequential mixed-methods design. We conducted a national online survey of parents aged 18–44 years (n = 510) and qualitative fieldwork with 74 parents across three regions of the country, including 44 in-depth interviews and 7 focus groups with 30 participants. Findings from the online survey indicate uneven awareness and perceptions: 62.9% (95% CI: 58.7–67.1) reported awareness of RSV, 53.5% (95% CI: 49.2–57.8) knew of available RSV immunization options, 88.6% (95% CI: 85.8–91.4) perceived RSV as severe, yet only 48.6% (95% CI: 44.3–52.9) perceived a high susceptibility to child contagion. High trust in and willingness to accept RSV immunization were reported by 72% (95% CI: 68.1–75.9) and 78% (95% CI: 74.4–81.6), respectively. Confidence in RSV immunization emerged as the strongest predictor of willingness to accept it, whereas perceived effectiveness of RSV immunization was the strongest predictor of confidence. Overall, willingness to accept RSV immunization is linked to the evaluation of its specific benefits, whereas confidence in RSV immunization is related to more general perceptions and positive intentions toward routine childhood vaccination. Qualitative data confirmed persistent knowledge gaps about RSV and underscored the role of emotions in shaping both trust in and willingness to accept immunization. Taken together, these findings suggest that RSV immunization strategies in Chile should simultaneously strengthen messages about the effectiveness of available tools and explicitly address parents’ broader concerns and past experiences with vaccination, offering concrete priorities for the design of future RSV communication campaigns in Chile and similar settings.
